19.1                  Introduction & Responsibilities

 

 

 

 

 

 

19.1.1               Purpose, Objectives and Scope

Purpose

  • To:
  • Minimize risk to personnel, property & the environment for ship & shore operations of ALMI TANKERS.
  • Evaluate all activities that could adversely affect Company’s operations and performance.
  • Take appropriate measures, to ensure the risk is:
  • Reduced or
  • Maintained at an acceptable level.

Objectives

  • To achieve an environment where:
  • Every individual is trained & motivated to personally manage risk in everything he does, on & off duty.
  • All operations and activities are successfully completed with the minimum amount of risk.

Scope

  • This Chapter describes the Risk Matrix methodology adopted by ΑLMI TANKERS.
  • It also defines, how the Risk Assessment and Risk Management methodology incorporates:
  • Company's own commitment for managing risk, &
  • External requirements, best practices and adopted standards on the matter.
  • Above external requirements include, but may not be limited to:
  • ISM code as amended
  • TMSA requirements
  • ISO 14001 (for aspects' significance evaluation) &
  • ISO 45001.
  • ISO 27001 (Information Security).

 

19.1.2               Introduction To Risk Assessment (RA) & Risk Management (RM)

General

  • Shipping is a high-risk industry.
  • Risk from shipping operations can be to:
  • Health.
  • Safety.
  • Environment.
  • Public disruption.
  • Company's reputation and/or Economics.
  • Data Information.
  • Treat any hazard identified, as an intolerable risk that is likely to occur.

Risk Assessment (RA) Process

  • The Risk Assessment (RA) process:
  • Involves examining an activity, where there is a concern that it could cause harm.
  • Enables to make decisions, whether:
  • Enough precautions are already in place, OR
  • There is need to take more precautions to prevent harm.

Risk Management (RM) Process

      Risk Management is an extension of the Risk Assessment process.

  • Risk Assessment process identifies if an intolerable Risk exists.
  • Risk Management (RM) process limits this Risk to As Low as Reasonably Practicable (ALARP).
  • It does so by:
  • Reducing or eliminating the likelihood of the incident/event happening, OR
  • Mitigating the consequences in case an incident/event does happen.

      For all practical purposes, consider the Term ‘Risk Assessment’ to include Risk management as well. 

     Correct application of the Risk Management process, will:

         • Reduce accidents and associated costs &

         • Thus, result in more efficient use of resources.

      In case of Information Security approach, it consists of the identification, assessment and evaluation of risks that arise from the transfer, management and storage of information.

19.1.3               Responsibilities

19.1.3.1              General Responsibilities

!!       Identification and response to potential hazards is an on-going responsibility of all personnel.

19.1.3.1.1         C.Ε.O/ Masters/ DPA/ Marine Manager/ Department heads

  • Responsible to propose and approve RAs and control measures.

      Department Heads may delegate the task of approving RA to Vessel superintendents.

19.1.3.1.2         DPA

  • Responsible to:
  • Develop, communicate, efficiently execute and ensure the ongoing effectiveness of the RA and RM procedures.
  • Manage the implementation of control measures.

19.1.3.1.3         Department heads and Masters

  • Responsible to:
  • Ensure:
  • Health and safety of the crew,
  • Protection of the environment,
  • Safety of the ship and the property.
  • Safe handling of sensitive information.

      Achieve above by:

        • Application of RA & RM principles, &

        • Evaluating risks & taking actions to reduce them.

  • Identify areas for improvement in existing RA/RM procedures.
  • Provide information, data and technical support for resolving hazards that they are aware of.

19.1.3.1.4         Risk Assessment Team

Requirements for RA Team

  • Includes 2 or more persons.
  • Includes at least one person must have received some form of risk assessment training.

      RA, though normally performed by a team, may at times be undertaken by an individual.

      Determine the no. & range of experience of people involved basis size & complexity of the analysed operation.

  • Where practicable:
  • Includes at least one person who is not involved in the scenario or incident under examination.
  • Involves work force representatives with "hands-on" experience, from an early stage.

      Individuals from third party organizations may also be employed.

Responsibilities

  • Responsible to:
  • Perform Risk Assessment.
  • Inform the Management:
  • Of the residual risks and hazards, that cannot be controlled or mitigated at their level, or
  • When risk outweighs benefit or
  • Of the need for any assistance, to implement controls.

19.1.3.3              Information Security Roles and Responsibilities

19.1.3.3.1         Information Security Officer

  • Responsible for monitoring that:
  • This procedure applies to all ALMI TANKERS S.A. information assets, &
  • All steps are conducted effectively.
  • Specifically, responsible for:
  • Ensuring that:
  • Business and legal requirements have been taken into account during the risk assessment.
  • All appropriate personnel are involved during the risk assessment phases.
  • Preparation of the asset model of all ALMI TANKERS S.A. information assets.
  • Analysis of the risk assessment surveys.
  • Maintaining the appropriate records.
  • Monitoring of the implementation of actions required by the risk treatment plan.

19.1.3.3.2         IT Department Members

  • Responsible for:
  • Identification of assets and their interdependencies.
  • Identification of the existing security controls.
  • Consultation during the threat assessment and vulnerability assessment phases.

19.2                  Levels & Types of Risk Assessment

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

19.2.1               General

  • In general, risk assessments are conducted, when the level of risk to life, health, safety or the environment, may be above acceptable levels, as:
  • Required by Company procedures or:
  • Judged by responsible Manager(s) or the Master onboard a vessel.
  • This part of the Chapter will define:
  • All the specific cases that require the implementation of the risk assessment process &
  • The documentation to maintain, for each of the above cases.

 

19.2.2               When To Conduct Risk Assessment

19.2.2.1              Levels of Risk Assessment

19.2.2.2              High Level or Fundamental Risk Assessment (Level 1 RA)

High Level Risk Assessments at the Foundation of the Company

  • At the time of foundation of the Company, Management has carried out High Level RA to identify:
  • All Routine activities/ operations that the Company/ Company Vessels would be engaged in.
  • Risk associated with those activities.
  • Control measures necessary to reduce Risk to As Low as Reasonably Practicable (ALARP)

     Control measures include Rules, Regulations & Industry Recommendations/ Best practices.

  • The control measures identified in the process have been used to develop a Management system which provides safeguards for all:
  • Shipboard activities/ operations.
  • Shore-based activities/ operations.
  • Two most significant aspects of these safeguards are SMS Procedures and Forms & Checklists.

High Level Risk Assessments for New Activities/ Operations

Responsibility: Company Management/ DPA/ Department Managers

  • Initiate a High-Level Risk Assessment whenever Company or Company vessels need to engage in New Activities/ Operations:
  • For which no procedures/ forms exist, &
  • Which are expected to be performed routinely. 

      This is covered under the ‘Management of Change’ process.

Naming the RA

Responsibility: RA Team

  • Give the Category Name as, HIGH-LEVEL RA followed by the type of activity/ operation.

      Document such risk assessments in RA-001 form.

Validity & Amendment of RA

      High Level RAs have no periodic validity.

  • Amend High-Level RA only if a review of the Generic RA for same activity/ operation indicates that an SMS procedure needs to be amended e.g., due to new hazards being identified or new controls required.

Limitations with High Level Risk Assessment

  • High level Risk Assessments cover the routine activities for which Risk is being assessed.
  • It may not be practical at this stage to identify:
  • Non-Routine Activities
  • All variables to the routine activities e.g., External conditions
  • For such activities/ operations, Activity Specific Formal Risk assessment (Level 3) is carried out.

19.2.2.3              Generic Risk Assessment (Level 2 RA)

      Generic Risk Assessments are derived from High-Level Risk Assessments for that same activity.

     Only difference being, the SMS procedures developed after carrying out High-Level RA are now used as ‘Existing Controls’ in Generic RA.

Process

Responsibility: Assigned Office RA Team

  • Carry out a Generic Risk Assessment for a new activity after:
  • High Level RA has been completed, &
  • The controls identified in High level RA have been used to create Procedures, Forms, Permits etc.
  • Reassess INITIAL Risk for the particular activity, now considering the Procedures, Forms, Permits as ‘Existing Controls’.
  • Create an activity specific Generic RA template.

     This template can be used by the Ship Staff (For Vessel RA) & Office Staff (For Office RA) as a base to carry out Formal RA (Level 3) prior to a ROUTINE activity on a particular day.

Naming the RA

  • Give the Category Name as, GENERIC RA followed by the type of operation.

     See examples on the type of Operation as categorized below:

        • Cargo/Bunkering operations (e.g., Loading, Hose disconnection, Discharging, Bunkering, STS)

        • Deck operations (e.g., Mooring, Anchoring, Helicopter landing, Brake holding adjustment)

        • Deck Maintenance (Replacement of mooring winch brake lining)

        • Engine room operations (e.g., Incineration, Bunker internal transferring)

        • E/R Maintenance (e.g., Piston overhauling, Exhaust valve replacement)

        • Accommodation operations (e.g., Cleaning of galley filters, Cooking)

        • Hull operations (e.g., U/W inspection, U/W propeller polishing)

        • Other operations (e.g., garbage disposal, Antenna inspection)

      Document such risk assessments in RA-001 form.

Validity & Review

  • Maximum Validity of the Generic Risk Assessments is as follows:

Overall Risk Level Identified

Validity

High

1 Year

Medium

3 Years

Low

5 Years

  • Review the Risk assessment prior expiry of validity.
  • Discuss the status of RA review during the Management Review.

      For further clarification on Filing see Appendix 3 - Clarification on Filing

Generic Risk Assessment library

  • A library with all generic risk assessments for routine operations is:
  • Maintained by the Company &
  • Made available onboard and ashore.

      See section  19.2.2.4.1 Risk Assessment (or review) for Routine Operations for details on how to use the RA Library.

19.2.2.4              Activity Specific Formal Risk Assessment (Level 3)

19.2.2.4.1         Risk Assessment (or review) for Routine Operations

  • Follow the Routine operations risk management process, whenever:

  • Master/ Dept. Manager has judged that above presents a threat to Safety, Health, Property, Reputation or Environment.
  • Initiate the risk management process as follows:

Process Flow – RA for Routine Jobs/ Activities

19.2.2.4.2         Risk Assessment for NON-ROUTINE Operations

  • Follow the Non-Routine operations risk management process, whenever carrying out Non-Routine operations which may involve hazards to:

 Health  Safety  Property  Reputation  Environment

     Typical examples of non-routine operations, requiring a formal risk assessment are:

         • Hot Work outside of the workshop onboard while vessel in normal operation (not during DD)

         • Punching of vessel’s transom markings, due to change of flag.

         • Relocation of Head Office premises.

         •Unplanned Maintenance of tank radar (additional to maintenance as per manufacturer’s instructions).

Process Flow – RA for Non-Routine Jobs/ Activities

Validity of RAs

  • Valid for the specific operation for which they were conducted.

!!       In any case not more than 3 months.

      When required, these RAs may be recalled and used as a basis, for a similar operation.

Naming the RA

  • Given the Category Name as NON-ROUTINE &
  • Document in RA-001 form.

      For the detailed process on conducting these RAs, refer to IMSM Chapter 19.3.

19.2.2.4.3         Risk Assessment as Part of the Management of Change

      All temporary, emergency and permanent changes or proposed changes:

        • Need to be evaluated & properly managed.

        • Are covered under the Management of Change process.

     This includes changes in the organization, its activities, new equipment, new material etc.

  • Use the risk assessment techniques for the significant changes, to:
  • Fully understand their impacts, &
  • Prioritise the most effective risk reduction measures.

Responsibility: DPA

  • Process a first level evaluation of the potential risk (especially for the Management of Change process).
  • Ensure the above is documented in the Management of Change (MOC) records.

      Depending on the above evaluation, a further risk assessment may be conducted.

      If so, document same in RA-001 form & attach it to the MOC record.

19.2.2.4.4         Post Incident Risk Assessment (Or Revalidation)

Incident during Routine Operation

  • If an incident occurs (including a near miss), during a Routine operation:
  • Consider amending the frequency of that occurrence.
  • Re-evaluate existing risk assessment.

      If an RA for the routine operation was not available, then initiate an RA.

Incident during a Non-Routine Operation

  • If an incident occurs during a non-routine operation, carry out a re-assessment of the operation.

     As the initial Risk Assessment has proven to be insufficient.

Initiating a Post Incident RA

Responsibility: Incident investigator and/or the DPA

  • Initiate an RA post an incident.

Documentation

  • For documenting these RAs, follow the typical routine or non-routine documentation process, that is appropriate for each case.

      For the detailed process on conducting these RAs, refer to IMSM Chapter 19.3.

19.2.2.4.5         Critical Equipment Identification Risk Assessment

  • The company uses Risk Assessment/ Management approach for identifying critical equipment and systems, including:
  • Ship specific critical equipment and systems identification.
  • Critical spare part determination.
  • Critical spares stock management and related processes.

      For these procedures, refer to IMSM Chapters 10.3 and 10.7.2.

19.2.2.4.6         Occupational Health Risk Assessment

Background

  • Health, ill Health and Safety are assessed for risk, as part of Routine and Non-routine RAs.
  • These processes ensure an ongoing:
  • Identification of hazards &
  • Determination and implementation of necessary controls.

      For the detailed process on conducting these RAs, refer to IMSM Chapter 19.3.

Establishment of Occupational Health and Safety Risk Assessments

  • The Company:
  • Is strongly committed to the protection of personnel’s’ and subcontractors’ health and safety, &
  • Has established dedicated Occupational Health and Safety Risk Assessments.

Description

  • These Risk Assessments:
  • Focus on the activities of each applicable rank/position or group within the company (onboard and ashore).
  • Assess each rank/position (or group), for health and safety risks associated within the normal scope of work assigned.

      OMR must always be part of the Risk Assessment team for these RAs.

Numbering of ORA

  • These RAs are uniquely numbered with a code always beginning with “ORA” (e.g., ORA-001).

Validity

  • Valid for 3 Years.

Review

  • Carry out Review:
  • Within their validity period of 3 years, for verification of their applicability.
  • Earlier (than above), in cases of changing circumstances.

     Including developments in legal and other requirements related to occupational Health.

Endorsing Industry Available Risk Assessment

  • There is official documentation available from well respected organizations involved in activities of assessing health and safety risk for personnel of the marine industry.

     Company considers such organizations to be IMO, ILO, OCIMF, Lloyds, DNV, ABS, BP, Shell & Exxon Mobil.

Responsibility: OMR

  • Review & assess such available documentation:
  • If considered acceptable, endorse same.
  • Assign a maximum validity of 3 years from the date of its introduction in the list of the ORAs.

      Endorsing such documentation as valid will mean that the control measures proposed are considered as adequate to reduce risk to acceptable (for Almi Tankers S.A.) levels.

  • At next review, substitute these ORAs by relevant RA-001 forms considering the initial documentations assessment.

      Follow review proces as detailed in IMSM Chapter 19.3.

19.2.2.5              Job Briefing / Toolbox Talk (Level 4 RA)

      These are meetings/ briefings (Formal or Informal) carried out in support of a Formal RA e.g. to review & discuss the procedures involved, implementation of the controls etc.

Job Briefing / Toolbox Talk

Participants:

     Supervisor (superior officer/rank),

     All involved subordinate members.

  Including any sub-contractors

When to conduct:

     Prior to operations onboard, &

     At the discretion of the supervisor, considering possible consequences.

Where to Conduct:

     At the site where the job is planned to be conducted among the people who will conduct it.

  If circumstances do not allow, same can be conducted at a remote location.

Scope:

     Describe the job / work / operation to perform.

     Discuss any:

•      Formal Risk Assessment conducted.

  If the task does not require a written Risk Assessment, then discuss possible hazards, precautions as part of an informal Risk Assessment.

•      Permit to Work system, if applicable for the job.

     Ensure that the subordinates/ contractors:

•      Understand the purpose/target of the job and responsibilities.

•      Have the ability (mental, skill, psychological, fatigue etc.), to perform the job.

•      Are aware of the actions and responsibilities in case of an emergency.

 

      Bring any information captured in the Toolbox talk to the attention of the Company, if it can improve Company Procedures.

19.2.2.6              Personal Assessment of Risk/ Take-5 (Level 5 RA)

  • This is Informal assessment of day-to-day risks carried out by each individual while conducting any tasks.
  • Typical Steps would involve:

 

1

Stop & Think

2

Identify all Hazards

3

Assess the Risks

4

Make the Changes

5

Do the Job Safely

19.3                  How to Conduct Risk Assessment

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

19.3.1               General – The Process Of Risk Assessment And Risk Management

  • Implement risk assessment and risk management, using the guidance and tools provided in this Chapter.

19.3.2               Step By Step

19.3.2.1              STEP 1: Define The Problem

  • Define the activity whose risks are to be studied.
  • Ensure that before initiating an RA, all parties involved have a common understanding of:
  • Goals
  • Methods to use
  • Resources required &
  • How the results will be applied.
  • In the dedicated field “Short description” in the Risk assessment form (RA-001), make a note of all:
  • Assumptions, &
  • Clarifications needed.

19.3.2.2              STEP 2: Identify Hazards/ Potential Incidents & Hypothetical Scenarios

General

  • Identify hazards, (potential) incidents or scenarios using a systematic approach.

Identification of Hazards

     What has the potential to cause harm?

  • Focus on factors that may cause an incident to occur, such as:
  • Human action/inaction,
  • Instrumentation,
  • Process equipment,
  • External factors,
  • Utilities.

      The hazard may exist in the current operation or it may result from changes to the current operation.

  • In broad terms, hazards can arise out of following sources:

 

CATEGORY

EXAMPLES

Programs:

     SMS Procedures not available

     SMS Procedures cover part of the task (WHAT, HOW)

     All Hazards not addressed in the SMS procedures

     SMS Procedures vague/ unclear, complicated

Work Environment:

     Weather - Adverse Weather/ Seas, Extreme Temperatures, Poor Visibility

     Vessel Location - Navigation Hazards, Regulatory Hazards, Security Hazards

     Task Location – Unsafe Atmosphere, Low Lighting, Noise, High Temperature

Equipment:

     Machinery, Equipment, Tools Defective

     Machinery, Equipment, Tools Inadequate for task

     Machinery, Equipment, Tools Difficult to use

     Equipment positioning or accessibility

People:

     Individual Basis –

•      Lack of knowledge/ skill/ experience in Task 

•      Physical/Psychological capability

•      Lack sufficient people for the Task

     Team composition Inadequate

     Social – Not getting along with people creating error traps like stress, time pressure, overconfidence, or poor communication

     Too many people not related to the task (distractions)

Processes:

     Process requiring Field Decisions – (if applicable, if needed, if appropriate, if desired)

     Mental or Physical Difficulty of Task

     Multiple Actions in a step

     Distractions due to multi tasking

Organization:

     Inadequate Work Standards

     Lack of Clarity in Roles / Lack of Supervision

     Inadequate Communication Internal

Responsibility: RA team

  • Consider the following (as applicable in each case) during the hazard identification process:

     Safety issues.

     The surrounding workplace.

     Design of work areas.

     Emissions.

     Work-related activities.

     Processes.

     Pollutants.

     Infrastructure.

     Installations

     Energy sources.

     Equipment.

     Machinery.

     Human behaviour.

     Materials at the workplace.

     Equipment etc.

     Human capabilities.

     Outsourced activities.

 

     See Appendix 1 - Examples of Hazards for an indicative list of categorized hazards, which may contribute to incidents.

Developing Hypothetical Risk Scenario

     What can go wrong?

      In this step, a detailed hypothetical risk scenario can also be deployed, describing:

         • Sequence of events leading to the incident, e.g., fire, vapor release, liquid spill, explosion, &

         • Consequences of the incident e.g., persons injured, environmental impact, economic impact.

  • Develop Hypothetical scenarios from conditions and failures/errors identified in the hazard identification phase.

      The process is more efficient if the scenario is as detailed as possible, to aid in estimating its severity and probability.

!!       However, do not make the scenario so detailed that:

         • It becomes trivial, &

         • The desired learning’s from the Risk Assessment is not obtained.

Risk Assessment Analysis Methods

     Appendix 2 -  Recognized Risk Analysis Methods  summarizes:

         • Some of the commonly used risk analysis methods, &

         • Key characteristics that:

            - Differentiate the various methods, &

            - Describe some of the commonly used techniques to identify hazards.

Responsibility: RA Team

  • Select a suitable approach/ method.
  • Take a brainstorming approach.
  • Use own experience and judgment supplemented by:
  • Incident reports,
  • Industry information, Experience etc.

19.3.2.3              STEP 3: Evaluate Likelihood and Severity of Consequence Under Existing Control Measures

19.3.2.3.1         General

  • To evaluate the Likelihood and Consequence of identified hazards, use:
  • Likelihood Determination, &
  • Severity (or Consequence) Assessment.

19.3.2.3.2         Likelihood (or frequency) Determination

  • Estimate how likely it is that the various incidents or hazards will occur.
  • Determine the likelihood based on the sequence of events in the hypothetical scenario.

      The Risk Matrix defines 5 likelihood levels based on the frequency at which the hypothetical scenario is likely to occur.

 

LIKELIHOOD LEVEL

1

Very unlikely - practically impossible

Could occur once or never in each vessel’s lifetime or for 20 years in the office.

2

Remote

Once per 10 years per vessel (or office)- The mishap scenario is considered unlikely. It could happen, but it would be surprising if it did.

3

Occasional

Occurring once every two - five years for each vessel (or office)

4

Frequent

Expected at least once per year onboard each vessel (or office) but not as frequent as monthly.

5

Very Likely

Expected at least once per month onboard each vessel (or office) or even more frequent.

 

Responsibility: RA team

Scenario

Actions

When selecting the Likelihood

     Discuss the scenario and the likelihood level & reach a consensus.

!!     If unable to reach a consensus, select the higher likelihood description under consideration.

To arrive at the scenario likelihood:

 

     Discuss and determine the likelihood of the scenario as a whole, or

     Discuss & determine the likelihood of the Initiating event, and then the likelihood of each subsequent event.

  Discussing individual event frequency/likelihood may be helpful when it is difficult to reach consensus

To determine the likelihood levels:

     Use own experience about the likelihood of similar events within the Company based on the history of all similar equipment or operations.

  Not simply the history of that particular piece of equipment or operation

     Use knowledge of similar events from the industry, when there is a lack of knowledge of similar events within the company.

19.3.2.3.3         Severity of Consequence Assessment

      Consequences are grouped into four general categories:

         • Health and safety of employees, subcontractors and the public.

         • Environment.

         • Economics/assets &

         • Reputation/public disruption.

  • Assign a severity level for each of the 4 categories based on the consequences identified in the hypothetical scenario.

 

SEVERITY LEVEL

PERSONNEL HEALTH / SAFETY

ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT

ASSETS

REPUTATION / PUBLIC DISRUPTION

1 - Minor

(Any failure that does not degrade the overall performance beyond acceptable limits – one of the nuisance variety).

Few minor injuries or insignificant illness. Ill health limited to a gloomy memory.

(Minor impact on personnel, temporary discomfort, first aid case, etc.). 

Minimum pollution / Little or no response needed.

(Up to 10 lt oil spill to the sea.)

(Unacceptable funnel emissions.)

(Accidental release of < 50 kg ozone depleting substances etc.)

Minimum cost / damage < $10.000

(Slight/Minor hull indents, equipment damages easy to repair by ship’s force, etc.)

Zero impact

(Minimal to none).

2 - Major

(Any failure that will degrade the system beyond acceptable limits but can be adequately counteracted or controlled by alternative means).

Number of minor injuries / Medical treatment for personnel

(No impact on public, laceration burns, concussion, serious sprains, deafness, dermatitis, works ­related disorders or other injuries leading to minor disability).

Little pollution / Limited response of short duration

(10-100 lt oil spilled at sea.)

(50-500 ozone depleting substance release.)

Little cost or damage ($10.000 – $100.000)

(Minor damages not affecting ship’s structural integrity or seaworthiness. Damage to equipment/systems needing extensive repairs).

Slight impact

(Minor disruption, Customers unsatisfaction /concern/complain).

3 - Critical

(Any failure that will degrade the system beyond acceptable limits and create a safety hazard).

Serious injury to personnel.

Non-fatal but serious ill health condition. 

(Limited impact on public).

Moderate pollution / Significant resources commitment

(100-10.000 lt oil spilled. Sensitive sea area at risk. Wildlife impacted.)

Moderate cost or damage ($100.000 – $1.000.000)

Considerable impact

(Significant disruption to small Community). (Customer evident dissatisfaction.)

4 - Catastrophic

(Any failure that can result in deaths or injuries or prevent of the intended mission).

Human losses / Fatalities

(Amputations, major fractures, multiple injuries, poisoning or other injuries leading to permanent disabilities).

Major pollution / Full scale response

(More than 10.000 ltrs, extended duration of response needed.)

(Wildlife Endangered species at serious risk.)

Extensive / high-cost damage >$1.000.000

(Loss of the ship or damages affecting ship’s structural integrity and/or seaworthiness).

Major National & International impact

(Significant disruption to Large Community). (Business continuity at risk.)

Additional Guidance in assessing Levels of above Categories

Category

Comments

Health and safety

     It is defined by the extent of injury to workers or the public.

  Usually, the workers are more likely to sustain injuries, however, in some cases the public may be more vulnerable.

Environmental impact

     It is best judged by the level of response anticipated by:

•      Amount of material released &

•      Environmental sensitivity of the area (where released).

  In an "Oil Spill" scenario, factor this into the severity, which will depend on the size of the community and the extent of disruption

Assets

     These are measured by the business loss due to the damage.

     As a guide, you may use the:

•      Approval levels for capital expenditures, to define severity categories, OR

•      Amount of time lost, for an approximate of the business loss i.e.:

-  4: More than 6 months.

-  3: Between 1 and 6 months.

-  2: Between 1 week and 1 month &

-  1: Less than 1 week.

Public Disruption/ Reputation

     It is defined by the scope of the disruption and the size of the population affected.

     It may also be judged by extent of Media coverage, i.e.:

•      National attention (Severity 4).

•      Brief national mention (3),

•      Local coverage (2), or

•      Minimal to no coverage (1).

Considering Consequences

  • On identifying a (hypothetical) scenario or hazard:
  • Consider the possible consequences in each of the 4 categories.
  • If there are consequences in more than one category, assign:
  • Severity levels for each applicable category, &
  • The overall severity based on the highest severity level from among the 4 categories.

     E.g., the economic impact of a non-gusseted, small pipe break on an acid pump would be low (1) but, depending on the scenario, the health effect could be high (3).

         In such case, select the higher level as the scenario severity.

!!       Be aware that when consequences in two separate categories have the same severity level, it does not mean that the consequences are equal.

     The purpose of providing different categories is:

         • To allow assigning a severity level to different types of consequence and to be further evaluated.

         • Not to equate health, environmental, public disruption or economic consequences with each other.

 

19.3.2.4              STEP 4:  Assess The Level of the Risk With Existing Measures

Process

  • Evaluate the relative risks associated with the events, after:
  • Identifying the hazards and potential mishaps or events, for a system or process &
  • Estimating the likelihood/severity of consequences, associated with the above events, under the existing control measures.
  • Use the Risk Matrix to assign risk (and making risk acceptance decisions) by using a risk categorization approach.

     Each cell in the Risk Matrix:

         • Corresponds to a specific combination of likelihood and severity of consequence &

         • Is assigned a priority number.

       

         It provides a framework to record Likelihood & Severity of Consequences.

         It may be used to:

         • Rank them in order of Significance.

         • Screen out insignificant ones, or

         • Evaluate the need for risk reduction of each Hazard.

Decision Matrix

Responsibility: RA team

  • First, evaluate the level of risk, based on the severity and likelihood as estimated by the RA process &
  • Then, categorize their possible combinations to be High, Medium or Low risk within the Risk Matrix.

 

RISK CATEGORIES

ACTION

LOW

TRIVIAL (1)

No action is required to deal with trivial / insignificant risks.

ACCEPTABLE (2-3)

No further additional controls / preventive and mitigative (P&M) or alternative actions is necessary. Consideration can be given to easily implemented solutions or improvements that impose minimal or no additional effort.

In case that the overall risk value is 1 – 3, the assessment is terminated.

MEDIUM

TOLERABLE (4-9)

For each scenario with this level of risk, efforts may be made to reduce risk to acceptable (low) level. If additional measures are not put in place, cautions required to ensure that all existing measures are well in place.

If the overall risk value for an operation is 4-9 the only acceptable way to proceed is as follows: A supervisor shall be assigned by the Master of Manager and all involved will be notified to proceed with caution being informed at the same time of all underlying risks.

HIGH

INTOLERABLE (>9)

Additional control measures are absolutely necessary for the work to be executed with only exception Master Making use of his overriding authority for the safety of life or protection of the environment.

 

  • For calculating the overall risk, take the highest of all risks calculated for each undesired outcome.

19.3.2.5              STEP 5: Identify Additional Control Measures (Managing risk)

Preventive or Mitigating measures

  • Establish additional control measures to temporarily or permanently reduce the risk for an operation.

      Two types of measures can be used to reduce Risk:

         • Preventive measures

         • Mitigating measures

        

          Preventive measures are preferred.

  • Use Preventive measures to reduce the:
  • Likelihood of One or more events in the scenario (which reduces the overall likelihood of scenario), or
  • Frequency of failures.
  • Use Mitigating measures to prevent accidents by reducing the:
  • Severity of consequences of accidents, or
  • Effect of failures.

 

Assessing Viability and Effects of Measure

  • Assess the Control measures, to determine whether they:
  • Are technically viable, &
  • Have significant effect.
  • Consider the effort required for implementing a risk-reducing measure in terms of:

Cost, time, difficulty, necessary resources, etc.

Vs

Benefit likely to achieve.

Selecting Measures/ Controls

  • Consider following factors when selecting measures, to reduce the risk:
  • Technical feasibility of the risk reducing measure.
  • The contribution of the risk reducing measure.
  • Effort and risks associated with implementing the measure, etc.
  • First, give attention to those measures, which have greatest effect in risk reduction for least effort.

Evaluating of Measures/ Controls

  • Undertake successive evaluations or risk-reducing measures, until reaching a point:
  • Of satisfying all the screening criteria (or dispensation given by Top Management) &
  • Where no further risk-reducing measures are reasonable.
  • When determining controls, or considering changes to existing controls, use following hierarchy:

 

 

  • When evaluating new control measures:
  • Ensure these are based on sound engineering principles and common sense.
  • Observe the following aspects:
  • Local conditions and circumstances.
  • State of scientific and technical knowledge relating to the particular situation &
  • Estimated costs and benefits.

     Examples of control measures are:

     Fire and gas detection systems.

     Temporary refuge.

     Fire-water systems.

     Evacuation systems.

     Active and passive fire protection.

     Oil clean-up and recovery equipment and procedures, etc.

 

  • During this step:
  • Validate effect of every measures on the assessment &
  • Reassess specific risk.

Deciding When to Stopping Implementing Additional Measures

  • Consider stopping the implementation of additional measures when the overall risk has reached:
  • Acceptable level, or
  • Tolerable level.
  • Follow decision matrix as detailed in (Step 4).

19.5                  Human Factors and Safety Critical Tasks

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

19.5.1               Understanding & Incorporating Human Factors

19.5.1.1              Defining Human Factors

  • Human factors:
  • Are the characteristics that affect human interaction with equipment, processes & other people.
  • Can include physical, psychological and social factors.

19.5.1.2              Human Error

General

  • Humans contribute to most incidents.
  • There is likelihood for human error, whenever people are involved in an equipment’s or process’s:
  • Design,
  • Construction or
  • Operation.

!!       This might lead us to think that people CAUSE incidents, BUT THEY DO NOT.

Facts that we need to Understand

  • People will make mistakes.
  • People’s actions:
  • Are rarely malicious, &
  • Usually make sense to them at the time.
  • Mistakes may be due to conditions and systems that make work difficult.
  • There is a difference between an ERROR & a VIOLATION:

 

ERROR

VIOLATION

     An action or inaction that unintentionally:

•      Results in an undesirable or unwanted condition, OR

•      Leads a task or system outside of limits, OR

•      Deviates from a rule, standard or expectation.

     An action or inaction that intentionally deviates from a rule, standard or expectation.

      Errors can be of 2 types:

        • Active Error: An action or inaction that results in immediate consequence

        • Latent Error: An action or inaction that results in consequences that are delayed.

 

!!       A large majority of the Incidents are caused by Systemically Driven Problems.

     To understand the underlying SYSTEM, see next section.

19.5.1.3              System Influencing the Human Actions

  • Human error, actions and decisions are often the result of the way the workplace is setup, i.e.:
  • How work, equipment and safeguards are designed, &
  • How leaders influence the culture in an organization.

 

      In other words, an individual is in the middle of a SYSTEM, that influences the way he decides & acts.

 

Factor

Examples

Overview of THE SYSTEM

Programs:

Clarity of Company Procedures, Guidelines etc.

These Factors influence each other & the Individual in the middle

Work Environment:

External Conditions like Weather, Lighting, Temperature etc.

Equipment:

Design, Condition, Ease of use etc.

People:

Influence of Other people involved in the Task.

Processes:

Processes are complex, difficult to understand or hard to perform

Organization:

Supervision, Leadership, Culture on board.

19.5.1.4              How Can We Find a Solution?

 

Solution

Description

Understanding:

     Understanding the conditions under which mistakes happen helps to present or correct them.

Using People to Identify Solutions:

     People:

•      Know the most about their work, &

•      Play a critical role in identifying solutions.

Design:

     Facilities, equipment & activities can be designed to reduce mistakes and manage risk better.

Supervision & Leadership:

     People in in charge of activities help shape the conditions they influence what other people do.

Learning & Improvement:

     It matters how persons in charge respond when things go wrong & that they take the opportunity to learn.

19.5.2               Safety Critical Tasks (SCT)

19.5.2.1              Definition

  • A Safety Critical Task (SCT) is a task:
  • Related to the ship’s main hazards, &
  • Where human error, action or inaction may cause or fail to avoid a serious incident.

!!       If actions or decisions of a human are the only protection against a serious incident, it may be only a matter of time before there is a mistake.

19.5.2.2              Identifying Safety Critical Tasks (SCTs)

General

Responsibility: Company

  • Identify Safety Critical Tasks where human error, action or inaction may cause or fail to avoid a serious Incident.

SCTs Identified by the Company

  • Company has identified following safety critical tasks.

 

  1.  

Berthing and mooring operations

  1.  

Cargo transfer operations.

  1.  

Double banking/ Ship to Ship operations.

  1.  

Tank Cleaning/ COW

  1.  

Bunkering

  1.  

Anchoring

  1.  

Operations Requiring Permit to Work (Hot Work, Enclosed Space entry, Working Aloft etc.)

  1.  

Maintenance of Critical Equipment

  1.  

Navigation

  1.  

Storing

  1.  

Tanker – Terminal Access

  1.  

Tending of Mooring Lines

  1.  

Lowering of Lifeboats {23.05.2023}

  1.  

Working on systems with the potential to move or the potential to release stored energy {23.05.2023}

19.5.2.3              Analysing & Managing Safety Critical Tasks

General

Responsibility: Company

  • For identified Safety Critical Tasks:
  • Identify opportunities for error and conditions that make:
  • Human error more likely, or
  • Consequences more serious.
  • Design tasks to eliminate or minimize error and error-producing conditions.
  • Identify barriers for the SCTs to reduce the likelihood or consequence of human error.

 

     Background Conditions that increase the likelihood of human failure

        These include:

        • Tasks that are complex, difficult to understand or hard to perform.

        • Insufficient training.

        • Parts of a task that are inefficient to do or where there is insufficient time available

        • Tasks or steps that are boring trivial or repetitive, unusual, infrequent or involve unfamiliar situations.

        • Inaccessible or hard to use controls,

        • Maintenance challenges from hazardous or moving equipment.

        • Difficult system or equipment interfaces, labelling. controls or alarms.

        • Unclear signs, signals, instructions or other information.

        • Reliance on error-free communications in prevailing noise and light auditions.

        • Working environment: noise, heal, lighting, ventilation, ease of access, visibility, line of sight.

        • Over reliance on recognizing emerging hazards, risk or change in a dynamic situation.

        • Multi-tasking or potential for interruptions or distractions.

        • Fatigue, stress and preoccupation

      For more details on identifying control measures, see IMSM 19.3 Section 19.3.2.5

Analysis of SCTs as part of High-Level Risk Assessment

  • Company has analyzed the identified SCT as part of High Level & Generic Risk Assessments.

      For more details on High Level & Generic Risk Assessment, see IMSM 19.2

19.6                  Job Hazard Analysis

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

19.6.1               What is Job Hazard Analysis (JHA)

  • Job Hazard Analysis:
  • Is a tool used to identify:
  • Potential Hazards &
  • Preventive or Mitigating measures
  • Has a narrower scope & is a less complex process than a Risk Assessment.
  • Focusses primarily on the injury related risks to personnel carrying out the job.

19.6.2               Which Jobs Require a Job Hazard Analysis

 

      Company has introduced ‘Job Hazard Analysis’ procedure to assess & address risks associated with Planned Maintenance (PMS) Tasks.

     For all the other operations on board, Company has:

         • Carried out a High-Level Risk Assessment to create Company IMS procedures, checklists, permits etc.

         • Provided a Generic Risk assessment library.

         • Established the Risk Assessment procedure (Routine/Non-Routine/ New Jobs).

  • Only PMS jobs require a JHA.

      JHA is used as a tool for preliminary assessment of all PMS jobs, to decide if a Formal Risk Assessment is necessary. For details see IMSM Chapter 19.6.4.

19.6.5               Periodic Review of a Job Hazard Analysis

Responsibility: DPA

  • Carry out an annual review of the Generic JHA library to:
  • Add any new JHAs to the library or delete obsolete ones.
  • Add any new hazards/ controls to the existing JHAs or edit as required.
  • Discuss the status in the Management review.
